metadata.title: Comprehensive Directory of Scrapyards, Auto Recyclers & Metal Recycling Facilities in North America, South America, and Europe
metadata.description: An enhanced, detailed directory of scrapyards, auto wreckers, salvage yards, and metal recycling facilities across Canada, the United States, Mexico, Brazil, and Europe, organized by province, state, and country. Includes contact information, accepted materials, and industry affiliations where available.
sources: Alberta Automotive Recyclers and Dismantlers Association (AARDA)
European Group of Automotive Recycling Associations (EGARA)
metadata.disclaimer: This directory is compiled from publicly available sources. Facility details, accepted materials, and affiliations may change. Verify all information directly with each facility before use.

mexico.description: In Mexico, scrapyards and auto salvage yards are commonly known as 'yonkes' or 'deshuesaderos'. The sector is largely informal, though the Mexican Institute for Recyclers (INARE) represents over 2,700 affiliated recyclers[reference:0]. Note that many facilities operate without formal registration, and environmental compliance varies significantly.

key_associations.name: Instituto Nacional de Recicladores (INARE)
key_associations.description: A civil association founded in 1994 that groups over 2,700 affiliated recyclers, including collection, handling, and recycling companies. INARE published an inventory of recycled materials in Mexico, including the ELV fraction[reference:1][reference:2].

key_associations.name: Asociación Mexicana de Distribuidores de Automotores (AMDA)
key_associations.description: Proposed an Official Mexican Standard for mandatory recycling of end-of-life vehicles and parts[reference:3].

brazil.description: Brazil's auto recycling sector is regulated by Federal Law 12.977/2014 (known as the 'Lei do Desmonte' or Dismantling Law), which requires dismantling companies to register with state traffic departments (DETRAN), issue invoices for each vehicle received, and formally deregister the vehicle[reference:20]. The sector is represented by ABCAR (Associação Brasileira de Reciclagem Automotiva). Despite regulation, only about 1.5% of the approximately 2 million vehicles reaching end-of-life annually receive proper recycling[reference:21]. The market moves approximately R$ 2 billion per year with 550,000 units recycled[reference:22].

key_associations.name: ABCAR (Associação Brasileira de Reciclagem Automotiva)
key_associations.description: The primary industry association for automotive recyclers in Brazil. ABCAR has facilitated international exchanges with organizations like Silverlake Automotive Recycling in the UK. The association estimates that R$ 14 billion in recoverable parts are lost annually due to inadequate recycling[reference:23][reference:24].

facilities.name: IGAR (Igarapé Reciclagens)
facilities.notes: Brazil's largest integrated vehicle recycler, inaugurated in February 2026. Investment of R$ 200 million. 80,000 m² facility generates 100-120 tonnes of scrap per hour. Can recover up to 80% of materials for new production cycles[reference:25][reference:26]

facilities.name: Renova Ecopeças
facilities.notes: Pioneer in vehicle dismantling in Brazil. Since 2011, has dismantled over 30,000 vehicles and reintroduced over 1 million parts to the market. New facility opened with capacity for 10,000 cars per year[reference:27]

facilities.name: Stellantis Vehicle Dismantling Center (Circular AutoPeças)
facilities.notes: Brazil's first OEM-operated vehicle dismantling center. Under the Circular AutoPeças brand, offers over 500 components including remanufactured, repaired, and reused parts. Part of Stellantis' circular economy push[reference:28][reference:29]

facilities.name: JR Diesel
facilities.notes: Founded in 1985 by Geraldo Rufino, starting with dismantling two crashed trucks. The family business evolved into OCTA Circular Economy Ltd, a company revolutionizing Brazil's automotive recycling industry[reference:30]

facilities.name: Kaiho Sangyo (Brazil Operations)
facilities.notes: Japanese automobile recycling company working to build an eco-friendly auto recycling value chain in Brazil, partnering with local garages and repair shops as micro, small, and medium enterprises[reference:31][reference:32]

facilities.name: OCTA Circular Economy Ltd
facilities.notes: Brazil-based company revolutionising the automotive recycling industry. CEO Arthur Rufino. There are over 3,000 yards in operation in Brazil, and the industry is gaining momentum with better inventory management and online sales[reference:33][reference:34]

europe.description: Europe has a highly regulated end-of-life vehicle (ELV) recycling sector, governed by the EU's ELV Directive. The sector is represented at the European level by EGARA (European Group of Automotive Recycling Associations), which was founded in 1991 and comprises national associations from 17 countries including Denmark, Finland, France, Ireland, Netherlands, Norway, Poland, Spain, Sweden, Belgium, Estonia, Germany, Switzerland, and the UK[reference:39][reference:40]. The EU-funded CarE-Service project and the newly formed ELV Forum are additional coordination bodies. France alone has approximately 1,700 authorised ELV centres[reference:41].

key_associations.name: EGARA (European Group of Automotive Recycling Associations)
key_associations.full_name: European Group of Automotive Recycling Associations
key_associations.description: Founded in 1991, EGARA is the European umbrella association for national associations of automotive recyclers. It incorporates one national and representative car-recycler association per country. Members include: England (MVDA), Austria (VöAv), Belgium (FEVAR), Denmark (DAG), Finland (S.A.L.), France (CNPA), Spain (AEDRA), Netherlands (STIBA), Ireland (IMURA), Germany (IGA), Norway (NBF), Poland (FORS), Switzerland (VASSO), Sweden (SBR)[reference:42][reference:43][reference:44].

key_associations.name: EuRIC (European Recycling Industries' Confederation)
key_associations.description: Brings together recycling federations from 20 EU and EFTA Member States. Represents the entire waste management value chain from collection and sorting to recycling, energy recovery, and final disposal. Actively involved in ELV policy development[reference:45][reference:46].

key_associations.name: ELV Forum
key_associations.description: A non-profit association established to strengthen coordination at European and international level and enhance members' contribution to the development and implementation of ELV policy. Founding members include ELVES (Ireland), Autorecycling (Slovakia), and Stiftung Autorecycling (Switzerland)[reference:47][reference:48].
